## Cutting Work

- [Activity-Based Plan](cutting-work/activity-based-plan.md) — A plan that lists what will be done rather than what will be delivered, and counts progress by activities completed; the plan can finish on paper with nothing received, and its reviews look for forgotten steps rather than missing features.
- [Catch-All Task](cutting-work/catch-all-task.md) — A task named by a broad quality is several unrelated pieces of work under one adjective; ask for the list, cut what can stand alone, and leave what only exists inside other work where it arises. The same words can still serve as a theme.
- [Choosing Between Splits](cutting-work/choosing-between-splits.md) — When a task can be cut several ways, prefer the cut that exposes something to throw away, then the cut that gives more equal pieces.
- [Combining Small Tasks](cutting-work/combining-small-tasks.md) — Tasks too small to stand alone are joined and estimated as one, preferring related ones because that eases prioritizing; bug reports are the common case.
- [Component Task Masquerading as a Unit](cutting-work/component-task-masquerading.md) — A work item that changes one layer or produces an artifact, presented as a unit of value; it is often made when a feature resists splitting and gets cut into its development activities, and the remedy is to combine it with its neighbours, because cutting it smaller cannot help.
- [Text Signs of a Compound Task](cutting-work/compound-task-text-signs.md) — Words in a task's title and text that suggest it holds several units; conjunctions, separators, generic terms, plurals and criteria that could each stand alone. A sign prompts a check that each part can be delivered on its own, and it does not prove the task must be split.
- [Deferred Concern Slice](cutting-work/deferred-concern-slice.md) — A task may be cut by leaving out a cross-cutting concern or a nonfunctional target, provided the first version says what it omits, the second version exists, and the first is not released alone.
- [Find the Core Complexity](cutting-work/find-core-complexity.md) — The meta-pattern behind the splitting patterns, used directly to find a first slice; locate what is most likely to surprise, list what there are many of, and reduce those to one.
- [How Far to Split Up Front](cutting-work/how-far-to-split-up-front.md) — Decide whether to enumerate all the pieces of a large request or cut only one or two, by whether starting the work will teach you what the work is.
- [The Humanizing Work Guide to Splitting User Stories](cutting-work/humanizing-work-splitting.md) — A coaching firm's guide to cutting large stories into thin vertical slices; nine patterns, a meta-pattern and two tests for choosing a split, grounded in practice and not in data.
- [Initial Task Inventory](cutting-work/initial-task-inventory.md) — A first pass that writes every likely task at a coarse level so that people see the shape of the work, walks the user's timeline to find them, and expects the list to grow; an entry is not yet a task.
- [INVEST](cutting-work/invest.md) — The six characteristics Wake named for a good story, what each letter claims, and which page holds the sign that makes it usable.
- [Planning Stops at Guesses](cutting-work/planning-stops-at-guesses.md) — Planning needs only enough design to name and size the work; tasks are guesses to be replaced when wrong, and the urge to draw a model during planning is the warning sign that planning has gone too deep.
- [Related Changes Temptation](cutting-work/related-changes-temptation.md) — Work added to an already sized task because it is nearby; it is kept only if it is necessary for the task or of equal priority to it, and otherwise it is ordered as a task of its own.
- [Right-Sizing, Not Same-Sizing](cutting-work/right-sizing-not-same-sizing.md) — Neither Little's Law nor limiting WIP requires equal-sized items, so cutting work merely to equalize size is the wrong fix while excess WIP and assumption violations remain; where a project estimates, the case for similar sizes on other grounds stands.
- [Spike as a Last Resort](cutting-work/spike-as-last-resort.md) — A time-boxed investigation is the right cut when a task is large because its implementation is poorly understood and no other split applies, and its acceptance criteria are questions; Cohn treats a spike as ordinary and pairs it with a placeholder, and where the unknown is the reach of a change in existing code it need not wait for the other splits.
- [Story Splitting Patterns](cutting-work/story-splitting-patterns.md) — The three-step procedure and nine patterns for cutting a too-big task into thin vertical slices, each pattern with the trigger that selects it, and Cohn's guidelines with the worked examples the first source lost; data boundaries, exceptional conditions, operations and CRUD, cross-cutting concerns, nonfunctional targets and mixed priority, plus cuts by case of the domain and by rising capability, which buy order and not reduced size.
- [Unit of Work](cutting-work/unit-of-work.md) — What this wiki means by a task, how that maps onto the sources' words "story" and "task", and the two working tests a unit has to pass.
- [User-Valued Features Over Isolated Tasks](cutting-work/user-valued-features-over-tasks.md) — Work is completed and delivered as features a user values, not as isolated tasks that only combine into value later.
- [Vertical Slice](cutting-work/vertical-slice.md) — A task cut through the architectural layers so that finishing it changes something a person can observe, as opposed to a task that changes one layer; Cohn's tracer bullet, which may show progress without yet being useful to its end user.
- [When to Split a Task](cutting-work/when-to-split-a-task.md) — Three triggers for cutting a task; it exceeds any iteration, it exceeds the room left in this one, or a decision sits close enough to its estimate that a better estimate would change the decision. A task above the ceiling must be cut before work starts and not when it is written, so one far from the top may stay large.

## Intake

- [Clarifying Questions](intake/clarifying-questions.md) — Read the repository first, then ask only what it cannot answer, about behaviour and failure, in terms the asker can answer; a question whose answer was in the code, or that the person cannot answer, is the sign it was wrong.
- [Closing What No Longer Applies](intake/closing-what-no-longer-applies.md) — An open item that has stopped needs a stated reason to stay; Kubernetes runs this on timers of 20, 30 and 90 days, which belong to that project, so what transfers is the triggers, the check that the need still stands, and a way to hold something open on purpose.
- [Defect Inside or Outside the Iteration](intake/defect-inside-or-outside-the-iteration.md) — A defect found in the iteration is part of the work that made it and finishes with that work; one found later is ranked like any other item, because outside an iteration a bug fix and a feature are the same kind of thing.
- [Duplicate Reports](intake/duplicate-reports.md) — A duplicate is closed against its original, and whatever it knows that the original does not is carried across first; the study behind this finds duplicates add information, and the test of a duplicate is one defect and not one symptom.
- [What an Incoming Report Must Carry](intake/incoming-report-content.md) — A defect report is fit to become a task when it says how to reach the failure, what happened and what should have happened; those are what the repository cannot show, and most other fields are recoverable, hard for a reporter to supply, or rarely used.
- [Issue Overload](intake/issue-overload.md) — More open items than anyone can keep in mind, which shows up as duplicates and forgotten work; the sign is new requests that repeat what is already there, and the source gives no count at which it starts.
- [Issue Triage Guidelines (Kubernetes)](intake/kubernetes-issue-triage.md) — The Kubernetes contributor guide to triaging incoming issues; a five-step process for one of the largest open-source projects, unsigned and unmeasured, of which the outcomes, the order of checks and the follow-up triggers survive at a few people and the groups, labels, bots and meetings do not.
- [Smells Depend on the Context (Montgomery et al.)](intake/montgomery-tracker-smells.md) — An interview study of 26 practitioners on 31 issue-tracker smells and 14 common problems; many smells drew "no" or "it depends", so a smell is a prompt and not a verdict. It gives signs with no thresholds, drawn from perceptions in mostly large companies, and no agent appears in it.
- [Reproduce Before Accepting](intake/reproduce-before-accepting.md) — A reported defect is accepted once someone has seen it happen; if it cannot be reproduced the findings go back to the reporter and it closes only by agreement, and a successful reproduction yields the check the task will be judged by.
- [Triage Procedure](intake/triage-procedure.md) — What to do with an item that came in; mark it as not yet looked at, take the oldest first, sort it into a few outcomes with the cheap checks before the costly ones, check the requester's classification, rate what is accepted, and set what follows up. Adapted from a very large project's process.
- [What Makes a Good Bug Report? (Zimmermann et al.)](intake/zimmermann-good-bug-report.md) — A 2010 IEEE TSE survey of developers and reporters on Apache, Eclipse and Mozilla, with a mining study of duplicates; it measures what experienced open-source people say helps, finds that reporters know what is needed and rarely supply it, and shows duplicates carry extra information.
- [Zombie Issue](intake/zombie-issue.md) — An open item nobody is acting on; it is the smell practitioners called most problematic, because what could have resolved it decays with time. The sign is an open item with no activity, and the source gives no length of time.

## Moving Work

- [Setting the Arrivals Column WIP Limit](moving-work/arrivals-column-wip-limit.md) — Derive the arrivals limit from average throughput divided by replenishments per interval, with a margin for variability; 5 items a week gives a limit of 5 weekly or 1 daily.
- [Artificially Aged Work](moving-work/artificially-aged-work.md) — An item that waits in a queue while others are pulled past it, or sits blocked with nobody working to free it, ages for reasons unrelated to its size and creates flow debt without any expedite lane.
- [Backward Movement](moving-work/backward-movement.md) — Moving a card to an earlier state loses visibility and data, so an expected cycle such as rework after review stays in the later state or goes to a new state on the right; the Scrum Guide's return of an unfinished item to the backlog is the one sanctioned exception.
- [Blocked Work Counts Against WIP](moving-work/blocked-work-counts-against-wip.md) — A blocked item stays in its column and counts toward that column's limit, so that being stopped restrains further pulling; moving it aside hides the stop.
- [Board Rules by Setup](moving-work/board-rules-by-setup.md) — The lookup from a project's setup to the rule that holds for moving, limiting and committing; two switches, a fixed period and a WIP control, resolve where Kanban and Scrum differ, and neither guide says when to pick the other.
- [Class of Service](moving-work/class-of-service.md) — A policy on the order in which committed work is pulled; it differs from a work item type, attaches only at commitment, differs from replenishment, and exists on any board with an order, declared or not. Vacanti treats it as a cost to predictability.
- [Conservation of Flow](moving-work/conservation-of-flow.md) — Work entering a process should leave it, so start work at about the rate old work finishes, from the outset, and finish what is started; arrivals outpacing departures grow WIP and Cycle Time until no delivery question can be answered, and abandoned work skews the data, though stopping work that is no longer needed is still the right call.
- [Constant WIP Throughout the Process](moving-work/constant-wip.md) — A limit on the arrivals column alone does not balance flow; WIP must stay constant on average across the whole process, by per-step limits, one global limit, or a mix.
- [Expedite Lane](moving-work/expedite-lane.md) — An expedite lane is exempt from the board's other limits and can block started work, so its own WIP limit, often one, is the only bound on the flow debt it creates.
- [FIFO Pull Order](moving-work/fifo-pull-order.md) — Once work is committed, pull the item waiting longest; strict FIFO is impractical, so the working form is mostly first-in-first-served. In Vacanti's simulation, changing only pull policy moved the 85th percentile cycle time from 50 to 100 days.
- [Just-in-Time Commitment](moving-work/just-in-time-commitment.md) — Work is committed to when it enters the process under explicit capacity, not when it enters the backlog; commitment means the item flows through to completion and a cycle-time range with a probability is communicated. Flow commits per item from measurement, Scrum per sprint from estimation.
- [The Kanban Guide (May 2025)](moving-work/kanban-guide.md) — The minimal definition of Kanban as a strategy for optimizing flow; it requires a stated workflow, explicit control of work in progress, a service level expectation and four flow metrics, and it gives no columns, no order and no period.
- [Multitasking](moving-work/multitasking.md) — Interleaving several started tasks; one study has value-adding time falling rapidly past two concurrent tasks for an individual, and even with no switching cost interleaving keeps each unit in process longer. Often set off by lateness, through requests for partial delivery.
- [Parking Lot WIP Limit](moving-work/parking-lot-wip-limit.md) — How to set a first limit on the parking lot from its own history, what the limit does, and what later fact shows it is wrong.
- [Parking Lot](moving-work/parking-lot.md) — A marked board area for items waiting on an outside party, with their time tracked; an item still parked past its expected end must become blocked. Wester rejects such areas, so this wiki narrows the parking lot to a declared exception under a WIP control.
- [Percentile Intervention Triggers](moving-work/percentile-intervention-triggers.md) — Compare each open item's age with the 50th, 70th and 85th percentile lines. Under an 85th-percentile SLE, the chance of missing rises from 15% at the start to 30% at the 50th line and 50% at the 70th, so each line is a checkpoint.
- [Process Policies from Little's Law](moving-work/process-policies-from-littles-law.md) — Little's Law's assumptions can be written as explicit policies on starting, finishing, unblocking and pull order, so that flow data becomes trustworthy.
- [Push Delays Defect Discovery](moving-work/push-delays-defect-discovery.md) — Pushing large batches or starting too much hides defects inside incomplete work, so they surface late; a pull system exposes them earlier.
- [Queue Buildup](moving-work/queue-buildup.md) — Started work piling up without finishing, which Vacanti treats as the observable form of poor flow; the project feels it as work taking too long, and iterations do not by themselves prevent it.
- [Reduce WIP Before Raising Throughput](moving-work/reduce-wip-before-raising-throughput.md) — When Cycle Time is too long, cut work in progress before adding hours or capacity, because added capacity usually raises WIP faster than it raises Throughput.
- [Slack for Expedites](moving-work/slack-for-expedites.md) — Delivering predictably with classes of service takes spare capacity, so study how often true expedites occur and design for that rate, for instance with lower overall WIP and free capacity helping work in process first; the source gives no formula.
- [Standing Expedite Lane](moving-work/standing-expedite-lane.md) — An expedite lane limited to one but never empty gives no fast path, only a renamed standard process and a worse one for everything else; a visible speed gap also invites every request to claim the lane.
- [Starting More Work When Cycle Time Is Long](moving-work/starting-more-work-when-cycle-time-is-long.md) — Responding to long Cycle Times by starting more items raises WIP and makes items take longer; lowering WIP is the first thing to consider, though the law alone does not guarantee that result.
- [Starting New Work When Blocked](moving-work/starting-new-work-when-blocked.md) — Reacting to a block by starting the next item raises WIP without finishing anything, and it looks like productivity on a points chart.
- [Tasks Are Not Assigned at Planning](moving-work/tasks-are-not-assigned-at-planning.md) — Cohn leaves tasks unallocated when an iteration is planned; a task gets its executor at the moment it moves to active and stays unowned and visibly available until then, and people take one or two related tasks at a time, because who should do what only becomes clear during the period.
- [Tests Specified Before Start](moving-work/tests-specified-before-start.md) — Cohn holds most cards out of In Process until a story's high-level acceptance tests are specified. It is a soft gate for people and a firmer one for an agent, which guesses at what it is not told.
- [What May Move](moving-work/what-may-move.md) — The trigger that lets a task start or change state; under the Kanban Guide a task starts only on a capacity signal and moves by stated policies, and under the Scrum Guide it enters by selection for a period, stays while the goal is safe, and leaves unfinished only by going back.
- [When to Use Class of Service](moving-work/when-to-use-class-of-service.md) — Start with no classes; build the process, operate it, measure it, and add one only if the data calls for it. For a single item, decide at commitment by comparing its due date with the forecast; if the forecast finishes first, it gets no preference.
- [WIP Control](moving-work/wip-control.md) — An explicit bound on how many tasks may be started and not finished; the Kanban Guide requires one over the whole workflow in any form, treats running under it as a departure too, and wants exceptions declared in advance, and Vacanti reaches it from the queue, with one count that both measures and stops.
- [WIP Lengthens Cycle Time](moving-work/wip-lengthens-cycle-time.md) — Work started and unfinished delays each new feature that must wait behind it; expediting past that queue pushes the problem onto the next feature. Cohn's cycle time ends at delivered value, not at a done column.
- [A WIP Limit Is Not WIP](moving-work/wip-limit-is-not-wip.md) — Having WIP limits does not guarantee Little's Law's assumptions; limits may be violated, may not change average WIP, and do not add up to the WIP actually in the process.
- [WIP Per Executor](moving-work/wip-per-executor.md) — Cohn limits each developer to one or two cards in process at a time, for flow and against context switching. The number is about people and sub-story cards; what transfers to an agent is one task per run, alongside a workflow-wide bound.

## Ordering

- [A Date Is Not Urgency](ordering/a-date-is-not-urgency.md) — A date on a task raises its urgency only if something outside the project changes at that date; such a date moves the task up the urgency bands as it approaches, and a date with no outside effect leaves urgency where it was.
- [Adding Scope to a Release Plan](ordering/adding-scope-to-a-release-plan.md) — New features enter a release after being estimated and compared on forecast value; the date moves only if the gain justifies it and the feature cannot ship afterwards.
- [Qualitative Cost of Delay (Black Swan Farming)](ordering/black-swan-qualitative-cod.md) — An unsigned article from a consulting site offering a three-by-three rating of value and urgency as a first step toward quantifying cost of delay; it reports no measurement, its matrix images are lost, and it is this wiki's main source on what comes first when value is hard to quantify.
- [Combining Prioritization Factors](ordering/combining-prioritization-factors.md) — Sort by value against today's cost for a first order, then move items forward or back for learning and risk; the people building may argue an item up, the owner decides, and an item whose result the owner could not be shown needs more than preference. Cohn keeps this informal, while a plugin has to write down each move or the order cannot be checked.
- [Conditioning Flow](ordering/conditioning-flow.md) — Among items near the top of the order, pull the one most likely to finish within the promised range, using current context such as an overloaded state, a soon-absent resource, or uncertainty that calls for a spike first; it can override strict priority order.
- [Cost Now Versus Cost Later](ordering/cost-now-versus-cost-later.md) — A feature that would cost more later is not automatically cheaper now; the early price must include later changes, a simpler version discovered afterwards, and complexity carried by all other work; cost alone favours late, while learning and risk can overrule it.
- [Cost of Delay Over Duration](ordering/cost-of-delay-over-duration.md) — Where durations vary widely and capacity is constrained, divide cost of delay by duration so that the work freeing most value per unit of capacity goes first; with word ratings the division has no arithmetic, so this wiki applies it only within one rank.
- [Cost of Delay](ordering/cost-of-delay.md) — What a piece of work loses by arriving later; it has two ingredients, value and urgency, which act on each other and do not add, it is usually a rate and not a sum, and it changes over time.
- [Critical Dependency](ordering/critical-dependency.md) — A dependency needs protection only if planned high-priority work cannot proceed without the deliverable, no other valuable work can be swapped in, and a partial deliverable would not let the receiver start.
- [End and Means Uncertainty](ordering/end-and-means-uncertainty.md) — What is unknown about a product divides into what to build (end) and how to build it (means); doing the work reduces both, and Cohn favours reducing end uncertainty early, since building the wrong product is among the largest risks.
- [Financial Measures for Comparing Themes](ordering/financial-measures-for-themes.md) — NPV, IRR, payback period and discounted payback each answer a different question about a theme's cash flow; none decides alone, and the chain needs money figures a board does not hold, so it applies to themes only when a person supplies them.
- [Handling a Sequence Dependency](ordering/handling-a-sequence-dependency.md) — When one task's size depends on another being done, leave the dependency if the wanted order already satisfies it and state the assumption; remove it with a stub only when the later task is really wanted first, and keep a zero-point task for the wiring.
- [Hand Off at the Iteration Boundary](ordering/handoff-at-iteration-boundary.md) — Commit only to work whose inputs are finished before the period starts; a commitment resting on something due mid-period is more fragile and puts the schedule at greater risk.
- [Incomparable Tasks](ordering/incomparable-tasks.md) — Tasks are incomparable when the rating ties them or cannot be made at all; a tie goes to duration and then to anything cheap, and a task that cannot be rated is not forced into a band.
- [Independent Tasks](ordering/independent-tasks.md) — Tasks should not overlap and should be orderable freely; a conditional estimate or a stated precondition is the sign that they cannot be, and work inside one task that restates another open task is an overlap found late, which can be held as a reserve until the commitment is settled.
- [Interrupting Started Work](ordering/interrupting-started-work.md) — Reordering unstarted work costs nothing, while stopping started work costs something; this wiki allows it only for a task at the top rank, against work rated well below it, and through the route the project's setup permits.
- [Just-in-Time Prioritization](ordering/just-in-time-prioritization.md) — Rank work only when the process signals free capacity, and only as many items as there are free slots; ranking deeper is waste because needs and knowledge change before the next pull.
- [Kano Model](ordering/kano-model.md) — Kano's model sorts features by how satisfaction responds to them; threshold features only prevent dissatisfaction, linear features pay in proportion, and exciters please when present and cost nothing when absent. It yields a category and not an order, a linear feature can carry a mandatory floor, one importance scale cannot see the reaction to absence, and categories decay over time.
- [Kano or Relative Weighting](ordering/kano-or-relative-weighting.md) — The source offers both and leaves the choice to the reader; this wiki resolves it by setting. Filter hard constraints first, use Kano where users can be reached and the question is what kind of need a feature meets, use relative weighting to rank what remains by value per cost, and use neither alone where urgency differs.
- [Kano Questionnaire](ordering/kano-questionnaire.md) — To place a feature on the Kano model, ask users how they would feel if it were present and if it were absent, cross-reference the two answers into one category, and read the distribution across some 20-30 users; two peaks in one row mean two populations, not a tie, and themes and skipping known answers keep the list short.
- [Lateness Passes Down the Schedule](ordering/lateness-passes-down-the-schedule.md) — A task with several prerequisites starts early only if all of them go well and starts late if any one goes badly, so dependent plans lose time and do not recover it; the asymmetry is structural and survives any executor.
- [Minimize Dependencies Between Features](ordering/minimize-feature-dependencies.md) — Features are written to reduce technical dependencies between them, because each dependency takes away a product owner's freedom to order by value.
- [Natural Order of Work](ordering/natural-order-of-work.md) — Most dependencies between stories just follow the order estimates assumed; working out of that order adds enabling tasks but rarely lengthens a project, and when it does the reason for reordering justifies it.
- [Order by Value, Not Convenience](ordering/order-by-value-not-convenience.md) — A plan that assumes everything will be finished has no reason to order by value, so it orders for the builders' convenience, and when time runs out the features dropped may outrank the ones delivered.
- [Ordering by Kano Category](ordering/ordering-by-kano-category.md) — Within a release, schedule all must-haves, then as many linear features as fit, then a few exciters picked with cost in view, and no indifferent ones, deciding scope before asking how long it takes; a must-have constrains what is in the release and not when it is built, past a base level more of it buys little, and a category is an input that a stated reason can override.
- [Ordering by One Factor](ordering/ordering-by-one-factor.md) — An order driven by value alone meets its derailing risk late, an order driven by risk alone builds what is later thrown away, and an order that counts time but not money overvalues features; each leaves a trace in board history.
- [Ordering by Value and Urgency](ordering/ordering-by-value-and-urgency.md) — When value cannot be put in numbers, rate each task on three bands of value and three of urgency, separately, and order by the combination; the bands are the source's, the two extreme combinations are the source's, and the order of the seven between them is this wiki's derivation.
- [Ordering for Early User Feedback](ordering/ordering-for-early-user-feedback.md) — Move forward the features that let real or likely users react, including those with significant user-facing parts, because this best reduces the risk of building the wrong product; it applies only if someone can react, and does not mean building the interface alone.
- [Prioritization Factors](ordering/prioritization-factors.md) — Cohn's four things to weigh when ordering work are financial value, cost, new knowledge and risk removed; the last two are what a sort by value and cost leaves out, and urgency is not on the list.
- [Prioritizing Infrastructure](ordering/prioritizing-infrastructure.md) — Infrastructure scores low on value, so it moves early only for a named reason; a cost saving net of later change and carried complexity, knowledge the work produces, or the risk of the component failing.
- [Priority Inflation](ordering/priority-inflation.md) — Most open tasks end up in the top band of the priority scale, so the band stops deciding anything; the sign is a top band that no longer separates tasks, and the source gives no figure for how full is too full.
- [Relative Penalty](ordering/relative-penalty.md) — Score what the absence of a feature would cost as well as what its presence gains, because work that brings no benefit but cannot be left undone is invisible to a benefit-only ranking; penalty is not urgency, and scoring it does not by itself guarantee a place.
- [Relative Weighting](ordering/relative-weighting.md) — Wiegers's method scores each feature 1-9 on benefit if present and penalty if absent, adds them, and divides its share of total value by its share of total cost; the percentages do not change the order, the score omits urgency, learning and risk, and it rewards cheapness.
- [Reprioritize Before Each Iteration](ordering/reprioritize-before-each-iteration.md) — Selection starts from a refreshed order and not last period's; feedback from the review can pre-empt items, and unfinished work is a priority decision and not an automatic carry-over.
- [Risk-Value Quadrants](ordering/risk-value-quadrants.md) — Sort features by risk and value into four quadrants; high-value high-risk first, high-value low-risk second, low-value low-risk last, and low-value high-risk avoided; value decides, risk breaks the tie, and positions change over time.
- [Sequence Versus Wait](ordering/sequence-versus-wait.md) — A sequence constrains order and leaves work available; a wait stops work on someone else's clock. A wait belongs between tasks, not inside one.
- [Sources of Return](ordering/sources-of-return.md) — A theme's return is forecast per period under four headings, new revenue, incremental revenue, retained revenue and operational efficiencies, and retained revenue can start before delivery; the requester should be able to quantify the reason.
- [Theme](ordering/theme.md) — A set of stories or features grouped because together they give a user or customer something of value; it is the unit compared when the value of one small task cannot be estimated.
- [Time Value of Money](ordering/time-value-of-money.md) — Returns arriving in different periods are not summed as they stand; each is discounted to present value at the organization's opportunity cost. The mechanism is sound, but over a two-year horizon its effect is often smaller than forecast error.
- [A Trade-Off Needs Cost and Benefit](ordering/tradeoff-needs-cost-and-benefit.md) — Decisions about what to do, delay or trim need estimates of both cost and benefit; estimates also let a feature be sized down, and customers only make these calls early if past estimates held up.
- [Uncertain Piece Goes Earlier](ordering/uncertain-piece-goes-earlier.md) — After a cut, order the piece whose duration is least known ahead of pieces already understood, so the uncertainty is removed while there is still room to act on it.
- [Urgent Versus Important](ordering/urgent-versus-important.md) — Value says how much a result is worth and urgency says how fast that worth drains away; they are rated apart because people conflate them, and two ratings that always move together are the sign they were not.
- [Value Decided at Replenishment](ordering/value-decided-at-replenishment.md) — Vacanti weighs value only when choosing what enters the process, and pulls committed work for predictability thereafter. This wiki resolves his objection to cost of delay by moment; ratings order what has not started, age orders what has, with a narrow exception.
- [Value Order Versus Technical Necessity](ordering/value-order-versus-technical-necessity.md) — The product owner orders by value but takes advice on sequencing; a value-ordered list cut at capacity must still be checked for low-ranked stories that are necessary, and those move up.

## Periods

- [6x2+1](periods/6x2-plus-1.md) — A macro-cycle of six two-week periods followed by a one-week period in which the team picks its own work; what transfers is reserved capacity for work the normal queue crowds out, and its failure is the short period becoming a dumping ground for earlier sloppy work.
- [Agile Planning](periods/agile-planning.md) — Planning as an activity spread across a project, producing plans that are cheap to change; Cohn's four defining properties and his plan-versus-planning distinction.
- [Bug Allocation](periods/bug-allocation.md) — Bugs enter a period as estimated work inside an amount the owner chooses; a new bug that must go in now is estimated and an equal amount of unstarted work comes out.
- [Changing the Plan Without Changing the Date](periods/changing-the-plan-without-changing-the-date.md) — When something is learned the plan changes, but the date is only one lever; scope can be dropped or reduced instead, and a change with no named learning is suspect.
- [Choosing a Buffer](periods/choosing-a-buffer.md) — Buffer only when uncertainty or the cost of being wrong about a date is high, match the buffer's unit to what is uncertain (time for schedule, features for scope), combine them where both are firm-ish, and skip buffers when no precise date and scope are needed.
- [Choosing a Service Level Expectation](periods/choosing-a-service-level-expectation.md) — Pick the percentile from the cycle time scatterplot together with whoever receives the work, usually starting at the 85th; it needs about 11 to 30 finished items from a process that obeys Little's Law, and three mistakes each have a sign.
- [Agile Estimating and Planning (Cohn)](periods/cohn-agile-estimating-planning.md) — Mike Cohn's practitioner book, here in a pre-publication manuscript, on planning as finding the best answer to what to build and by when; it keeps size apart from duration, derives dates from a measured rate, states uncertainty and replans each iteration. It is the wiki's largest source, written for human teams on iterations, with no agent in it and no measurement of its own.
- [Commitment Over a Period](periods/commitment-over-a-period.md) — What a project actually promises; the Scrum Guide commits to a Sprint Goal and only forecasts the items, Cohn commits to the functionality of the selected stories and keeps the goal loose, the Kanban Guide has no period and forecasts per item, and under every setup a list of sub-steps is never the commitment.
- [Date-Driven Versus Feature-Driven](periods/date-driven-vs-feature-driven.md) — The test for which factor is fixed in a release, the date with scope negotiable or a feature set with the date following from it, and which computation each one takes.
- [Deriving Duration from Velocity](periods/deriving-duration-from-velocity.md) — Sum the size of the desired work, divide by velocity to get iterations, round deliberately, and map the result onto a calendar.
- [Droppable Stories as a Schedule Buffer](periods/droppable-stories-as-a-schedule-buffer.md) — When a forecast leaves no margin, name about one period's velocity of low-priority stories, do them last, and drop them if time runs out; otherwise tell people the date may move. It is a feature buffer named late, not the time reserve of a schedule buffer.
- [End-of-Period Crunch](periods/end-of-period-crunch.md) — Too long a period produces a relaxed start and a frantic end; the remedy is a length that spreads pressure evenly, not more pressure, and the opposite failure is a period so short it stays hectic with no recovery.
- [Feature Buffer](periods/feature-buffer.md) — Planning for mandatory work plus 25-40% optional work, built last, so a firm date can be met by dropping the optional part; DSDM's MoSCoW caps Must Have at 70% of effort for the same effect.
- [Feeding Buffer](periods/feeding-buffer.md) — Reserved time in the delivering team's plan that protects another team's start date from a late hand-off, added after reducing dependencies, sized at about 50 percent by default, and rarely longer than an iteration.
- [Filling a Period](periods/filling-a-period.md) — How much to select for an iteration; the Scrum Guide names three inputs, past performance, upcoming capacity and the Definition of Done, and gives no formula, while Cohn's case fills one story at a time, stops at the tightest stage and not at the total, and leaves room to add. Selection applies only under an iteration setup.
- [Fitting Stories into a Release](periods/fitting-stories-into-a-release.md) — The procedure for filling a release; iterations times velocity gives capacity, stories are counted off an ordered list, and the result is tested against the release's conditions, worked through the SwimStats numbers.
- [Fixed Date, Variable Scope](periods/fixed-date-variable-scope.md) — Cohn's timed-race view of a project; the end date is known and what will be delivered by it is not, so planning means revising goals against the date.
- [Forecast Assumption Mismatch](periods/forecast-assumption-mismatch.md) — A forecast is wrong when the model or its tool assumes a policy the process does not follow; one unmodelled pull order moved an 85th-percentile forecast from 65 to 100 days in Vacanti's scenario.
- [Forecasting from an Average](periods/forecast-from-an-average.md) — A date derived from a mean carries no probability, because the mean's percentile is unknown until the distribution is known.
- [A Forecast Needs a Stable Process](periods/forecast-needs-a-stable-process.md) — Past flow data predicts the future only from a stable process; arrivals far outpacing departures, or a triangle-shaped Cycle Time scatterplot, say to question the data before forecasting from it.
- [A Forecast Carries a Range and a Probability](periods/forecast-range-and-probability.md) — Vacanti calls a date a forecast only if it states both a range and the probability of landing in it, computed from recorded data; the sign is a date with neither, and this wiki resolves it against Cohn's range-or-confidence by what the project has recorded.
- [Iterating Reduces Uncertainty](periods/iterating-reduces-uncertainty.md) — Uncertainty about what to build and about how to build it are both reduced by iterating; show working results to users, and feed what is learned back into the plan. A plan that never changes across cycles is not getting the benefit.
- [Iteration Boundary Day](periods/iteration-boundary-day.md) — Where an iteration starts in the week is a choice; Cohn's example team moved to Friday-to-Thursday so a Friday release had the quiet weekend as a buffer, with Friday morning absorbing leftovers.
- [Iteration Capacity](periods/iteration-capacity.md) — Plan against what is left after standing obligations are taken out, not against nominal hours; Cohn's team of seven plans 4 to 6 hours a person a day, 280 to 420 of 560 hours, his case study assumes six and its people doubt it, and unpredictable support comes out first.
- [Iteration Length Versus Cycle Time](periods/iteration-length-versus-cycle-time.md) — Compare a period's length with Cycle Time percentiles to learn the chance a story started on day one finishes inside it; if the 85th percentile exceeds the period, the period's commitment is not credible as stated.
- [Iteration Plan Versus Release Plan](periods/iteration-plan-versus-release-plan.md) — Cohn's two stages of agile planning; a coarse release plan over months and a detailed iteration plan made as the iteration starts, which exists to refine the release plan's guesses with what has since been learned.
- [Mid-Period Change](periods/mid-period-change.md) — During a period the commitment is protected; the Scrum Guide protects a goal and lets the list of work change, Cohn protects the selected features and limits the period by how long priorities hold, and the setup decides which applies. A change that endangers the commitment waits, and a goal gone obsolete is cancelled openly and not quietly replaced.
- [Monte Carlo Simulation](periods/monte-carlo-simulation.md) — Forecasting a finish by sampling real flow data many times; the output is a set of outcomes with probabilities and not one date, Siemens HS committed near the 85th percentile, and the method is only as good as its data, its assumptions and the stability of the history behind it.
- [When Multi-Team Planning Techniques Apply](periods/multi-team-techniques-scale-limit.md) — Cohn's four multi-team techniques are added only as needed, and by his own account a single team needs none of them, so they are not applied to a few people as ritual.
- [Narrowing a Task Mid-Period](periods/narrowing-a-task-mid-period.md) — When a task proves larger than planned during a period, whoever owns scope decides at once to move it out, split it, or reduce its acceptance criteria; the standard of done is never what gives.
- [New Idea Latency](periods/new-idea-latency.md) — Under a fixed period, an idea arriving at a random moment reaches working software after 1.5 period lengths on average; half a period waiting for the next start and one full period to build it.
- [No Planning or Over-Planning](periods/no-planning-or-over-planning.md) — Two opposite responses to plans being wrong; skipping planning, so basic date questions go unanswered, or planning so heavily that thoroughness is mistaken for accuracy.
- [Period Length](periods/period-length.md) — A period has a fixed length of one month or less, in practice one to four weeks, chosen per project from how long a goal stays valid, how often results can be reviewed and Cohn's seven factors, then held; work is sized to the period and never the period to the work, and two weeks is one practitioner's preference with stated conditions.
- [Plan Deliberately Overstated](periods/plan-deliberately-overstated.md) — Dates or scope known to be unrealistic are stated so that a partial result looks acceptable; the plan stops being a forecast, and comparing it with fact shows nothing.
- [Planned Velocity](periods/planned-velocity.md) — Before any iteration has finished, the points committed to the first iteration stand in for velocity as a labelled guess until observed values replace it; it ranks behind waiting for one or three iterations, and its result goes out as a range.
- [Planning Horizons](periods/planning-horizons.md) — Plan at the release, iteration and day levels, with detail shrinking as the horizon nears and each level doing a different job, so none replaces another; a plan that runs past what can be seen needs built-in points to look again.
- [Potentially Shippable Increment](periods/potentially-shippable-increment.md) — Each iteration ends with features coded, tested and of releasable quality; the test is whether the team could ship, not whether it did.
- [Project Buffer Sizing](periods/project-buffer-sizing.md) — Sizing a schedule buffer as the square root of the sum of squared 50-to-90 spreads, so that riskier items weigh more; or, failing two estimates, half the sum of 50% estimates, which ignores where the risk is.
- [Purpose of Planning](periods/purpose-of-planning.md) — Cohn's claim that planning exists to answer what to build and not only to produce a date, and the five things a planning process supports, each filtered here for what survives a few people steering an agent.
- [Quarter-End Release Date](periods/quarter-end-release-date.md) — Do not aim a release or period end at a date where value steps down, such as a fiscal quarter end; Cohn's one-week slip past March 31 cost a full quarter's revenue recognition, and month-aligned periods hit a quarter end every third period.
- [Reforecasting a Release from Velocity](periods/reforecasting-a-release-from-velocity.md) — Divide remaining points by measured velocity, round up to whole periods, add elapsed periods, and repeat after every period and every scope change; rounding up leaves only the margin the fraction happens to give.
- [Release Plan Level of Detail](periods/release-plan-level-of-detail.md) — A release plan holds stories, not tasks, assignees or in-iteration order, places work into named iterations only for the near term, because later detail is planned with less knowledge than it will have, and needs its detail in two places, what comes next and what may not make it.
- [Release Plan](periods/release-plan.md) — A high-level plan over a period longer than an iteration; a list of stories, its assumptions, and the destination that keeps iterations from being a sequence of false peaks.
- [Release Versus Iteration](periods/release-versus-iteration.md) — An iteration is a timebox; a release is a set of related functionality built across iterations. What ends the unit, a date or a content set, separates them.
- [Rolling Lookahead Plan](periods/rolling-lookahead-plan.md) — A release plan that shows detail only for the next two or three iterations and drops completed ones; the window's length follows how often and how heavily work depends across streams.
- [Schedule Buffer](periods/schedule-buffer.md) — Protecting a firm date by planning from 50% estimates and adding one shared project buffer of time, so that the plan guards the overall deadline rather than each task.
- [The 2020 Scrum Guide](periods/scrum-guide-2020.md) — The definition of Scrum by Schwaber and Sutherland; mostly accountabilities and events, which this wiki drops, and a small core about the Sprint, the Sprint Goal, selection and the Definition of Done that it keeps. It has no board, no states and no limit on concurrent work.
- [Service Level Expectation](periods/service-level-expectation.md) — A per-item statement of how long an item should take from started to finished, as an elapsed time and a probability read from cycle time history; the Kanban Guide calls it a forecast and Vacanti a small-c commitment owed at the moment of pulling, it carries no penalty, and its example figures are not targets.
- [Forecasting a Single Item from Cycle-Time Percentiles](periods/single-item-forecast.md) — To forecast one item, epic or project, collect the cycle times of finished items of the same type, pick a percentile, and state the corresponding range with that probability.
- [Service Level Expectations by Work Item Type](periods/sle-by-work-item-type.md) — Cycle time data can be filtered by type and different SLEs offered, but each subtype must then obey Little's Law separately. Start with one global SLE; split only once the whole system is predictable and the split is needed.
- [Stating Plan Uncertainty](periods/stating-plan-uncertainty.md) — A schedule or release forecast carries its uncertainty as a range or a confidence, plus its basis, on whichever of scope or date is not fixed, in units as coarse as the uncertainty; a bare date or a fractional iteration count claims a precision the plan's inputs do not have.
- [Straight-Line Projection of a Release Date](periods/straight-line-projection.md) — Extending a throughput trend line to the backlog line yields a date with no probability, built on an average and on a shape that is usually an S-curve; tolerable as a gut check, and under iterations only in range form.
- [Timeboxed Iteration](periods/timeboxed-iteration.md) — An iteration ends on its date even if functionality is dropped; all kinds of work happen inside it, not in phases across iterations.
- [Unfinished at Period End](periods/unfinished-at-period-end.md) — A task that has not met the standard of done is not partly done; it goes back to be ordered again, it is not carried over automatically, and it does not count toward what the period finished. Cohn agrees and adds a reason, that each period is planned afresh, which removes the work's claim on the next period but not the partial work.
- [Updating the Release Plan](periods/updating-the-release-plan.md) — A release plan is revisited on a regular cadence; after each iteration by default, and up to four to six weeks only while velocity holds and iteration planning brings no surprises.
- [Utilization Versus Slack](periods/utilization-versus-slack.md) — Loading to full capacity leaves nothing to absorb the variability of real tasks; keep a margin. The source gives the reasoning and an analogy, and no figure for the margin.
- [Velocity Range Forecast](periods/velocity-range-forecast.md) — Forecast from three velocity values (most recent, mean of up to the last eight, mean of the slowest three) to get a range of work by a date or of iterations for a scope, never one number.
- [Velocity Versus Commitment Planning](periods/velocity-versus-commitment-planning.md) — Two ways to fill an iteration; sum story estimates to last period's velocity, or add stories one at a time until the team can commit no further. Cohn prefers commitment because 3 to 12 stories are too few for estimate errors to average out, so velocity gauges progress against the release and is not a fill line for the next period.

## Reading History

- [Accounting for Abandoned Work](reading-history/accounting-for-abandoned-work.md) — When started work is dropped, do not delete it; move it to the finished state, record the date, and tag it as abandoned, so analytics can include or filter it and cumulative flow diagrams stay valid.
- [Actionable Metrics](reading-history/actionable-metrics.md) — A test for whether a metric earns its place; it suggests a specific intervention, it predicts something asked of the project, and it costs little to collect, and a metric that changes no decision over several periods is dropped.
- [All-or-Nothing Counting](reading-history/all-or-nothing-counting.md) — A task counts toward velocity at its full estimate if complete at period end and not at all otherwise; partial credit is rejected because only not started and done can be known, so a credited fraction puts a guess into the rate, and because it hides a growing stock of unfinished work. The rule needs a done that can pass or fail.
- [Approximate Average Cycle Time](reading-history/approximate-average-cycle-time.md) — The horizontal distance on a CFD gives an approximate average Cycle Time for finished items, not an exact Cycle Time and not an exact average, because the items entering at one end are not necessarily those leaving at the other.
- [Approximate Versus Actual Average Cycle Time](reading-history/approximate-versus-actual-cycle-time.md) — Compare the average Cycle Time read off a CFD with the exact average from the same data; greater means accumulating flow debt, less means repaying it, roughly equal means neither.
- [Board Misuse Corrupts Flow Data](reading-history/board-misuse-corrupts-flow-data.md) — Flow data can be no better than the use of the board that produced it. Late updates, uncaptured blockers and random moves leave history that must be repaired or thrown away.
- [Capturing Flow Data](reading-history/capturing-flow-data.md) — Flow analytics need one record per item holding the date it entered each workflow step, plus attributes that later serve as filters, including how the item ended.
- [Chosen Delay Versus Slip](reading-history/chosen-delay-versus-slip.md) — Before calling a release late, check which date people were told, whether scope changed by a recorded decision, and whether the earlier date was still available; a later finish with none of these is a slip.
- [Cycle Time Adds One Time Unit](reading-history/cycle-time-add-one-time-unit.md) — Vacanti counts Cycle Time inclusively, adding one reporting unit to the date subtraction, so same-day work is one unit rather than zero. Consistency matters more than the convention, and the rule applies to Cycle Time, not to the Throughput run.
- [Cycle Time Percentile Lines](reading-history/cycle-time-percentile-lines.md) — Horizontal lines at chosen percentiles of finished items' cycle times, usually 50, 70, 85 and 95; they need no assumption about the distribution, resist outliers, and turn history into a time-plus-probability statement.
- [Cycle Time](reading-history/cycle-time.md) — Cycle Time is the elapsed time a work item spends as WIP; it is measured in calendar time rather than active time because customers think in dates and most unpredictability sits in the waits, and names like Lead Time only mean anything once boundaries are stated.
- [Diagnosing Unfinished Work](reading-history/diagnosing-unfinished-work.md) — A task left unfinished at period end has at least three candidate causes, too large, underestimated or too much selected, and each points to a different fix, which matters more than how the task is counted.
- [Flow Debt](reading-history/flow-debt.md) — Cycle Time taken from some in-progress items to finish others sooner; it is repaid as longer Cycle Times or discarded work, and either way as less predictability.
- [Flow Efficiency](reading-history/flow-efficiency.md) — Flow Efficiency is active or touched time as a percentage of total Cycle Time, computed at Siemens HS from queue states plus blocked time; a low ratio says improvement lies in the waits and not the work, and its input needs a board whose states separate waiting from working.
- [Flow Metrics](reading-history/flow-metrics.md) — What the flow measures count and do not; the Kanban Guide requires WIP, Throughput, Work Item Age and Cycle Time, Vacanti treats three of them as common to all flow implementations and claims a chain between them, and all can be read from board history without logged hours.
- [Gap on a Scatterplot](reading-history/gap-on-a-scatterplot.md) — A gap means nothing finished in that interval, and it lines up with a flat bottom line on the CFD; stacks at sprint boundaries with thin data between them are the batch-transfer form.
- [Good Plan Test](reading-history/good-plan-test.md) — A plan is judged by whether it was reliable enough to decide on, not by accuracy; six months delivered in seven was still useful, in twelve was not, and regular updates are part of the verdict.
- [Hedge, Speculative or Ponzi Flow Debt](reading-history/hedge-speculative-ponzi.md) — Questions about expedite frequency, limit adherence and pull policy that place a board's borrowing in one of Minsky's three debtor types, to answer whether its flow debt can be repaid.
- [How Much Flow Data Is Enough](reading-history/how-much-flow-data.md) — Far fewer finished items than people assume are enough to start reading a process; five bracket the median at 93.75%, the source's eleven-sample figure needs correcting, and a small sample says little about the tail.
- [Individual Velocity](reading-history/individual-velocity.md) — Velocity split by person measures the wrong thing and, per Cohn, rewards finishing alone over helping and teaches people to hold finished work until its deadline, which corrupts board history. The plugin reports for the project and not per person. His supporting claim that stories should need several people does not transfer to an agent.
- [Internal and External Variability](reading-history/internal-and-external-variability.md) — Moving up a scatterplot's stack, long cycle times tend to have causes outside the team; moving down, causes the team controls. Outliers are kept and investigated, and items just past a percentile line are the actionable ones.
- [Iteration Summary of Plan Versus Fact](reading-history/iteration-summary-plan-versus-fact.md) — A per-story table of result, points planned and points earned shows plan against fact for an iteration; unfinished work earns zero and an overrun is recorded as text, so the total is the iteration's velocity.
- [Checking Little's Law's Assumptions](reading-history/littles-law-assumptions.md) — Which assumptions a flow calculation needs depends on the form of the law and on whether WIP reached zero; each throughput-form assumption can be checked against board history for a chosen window, and three of them double as an audit of a process's policies.
- [Little's Law Does Not Forecast](reading-history/littles-law-does-not-forecast.md) — The law is exact only looking back over a completed period and is a relationship of averages; use it for measurement and rough gut-checks, and never as the basis of a commitment.
- [Little's Law](reading-history/littles-law.md) — The relationship of averages that locks WIP, Cycle Time and Throughput together over a completed period; its practical value lies in its assumptions and not its arithmetic.
- [Low Cycle Time Cluster](reading-history/low-cycle-time-cluster.md) — A tight group of unusually low dots is a question, not good news; a temporary surge in capacity produces it, and the skewed data then flows into forecasts and service levels.
- [Measuring Arrival and Departure Rates](reading-history/measuring-arrival-and-departure-rates.md) — Count items crossing the arrival and departure points per unit of time, in the same unit, then compare the averages; a shared reporting unit does not require a shared cadence.
- [Non-Standard Departure](reading-history/non-standard-departure.md) — How to record an item that leaves a step other than by finishing it; tag a departure into Done when the work is over, erase the entry date when the arrival was a mistake or the item will return, and never decrement a count.
- [Partial Credit for Unfinished Tasks](reading-history/partial-credit-for-unfinished-tasks.md) — A task unfinished at a period's close earns no velocity by default; only when the remainder will not be done next period is it split, with the done part and the rest estimated separately and no need to sum to the original.
- [Percentile Spread](reading-history/percentile-spread.md) — A wide gap between cycle time percentile lines signals process variability and makes each extra point of confidence expensive. The improvement aim is to shift all the lines down and close the gaps.
- [Plan Conformance as Success](reading-history/plan-conformance-as-success.md) — Scoring a project by on-time, on-budget, all-original-features rewards keeping mediocre items and ignores the main risk, building the wrong product; a plan never revised after learning is the warning sign.
- [Predictability](reading-history/predictability.md) — How accurately a process answers "When will it be done?"; Vacanti scores it by that accuracy and not by adherence to a practice, widens it to a system behaving as expected, and treats it as the result of policies a project sets, written or not.
- [Reading a Cycle Time Scatterplot](reading-history/reading-a-cycle-time-scatterplot.md) — A procedure for turning the shapes on a cycle time scatterplot into questions about the policy that produced them; the chart shows variation but does not classify it.
- [Reading Flow Metrics off a CFD](reading-history/reading-flow-metrics-off-a-cfd.md) — The procedure for reading WIP (vertical), Approximate Average Cycle Time (horizontal, backward, plus one unit) and exact average Throughput or arrival rate (slope) from a valid CFD, overall or between any two lines.
- [Forces on Release Progress](reading-history/release-progress-forces.md) — Work remaining in a release changes through three separate forces, work completed, requirements added or removed, and estimates revised, so explaining plan against fact means splitting a change in remaining work into these three before judging it.
- [Replanning on New Knowledge](reading-history/replanning-on-new-knowledge.md) — A plan is a point-in-time guess; at each iteration start, what was learned about progress and about value is folded in, and a release plan resting on outdated information or false assumptions is updated, while priorities stay relatively stable between iterations.
- [Siemens HS Case Study](reading-history/siemens-hs-case.md) — The setting, timeline and numbers of Siemens Health Services' move from points and velocity to WIP, Cycle Time and Throughput, with the chapter's internal inconsistencies recorded.
- [Signs of Poor Flow](reading-history/signs-of-poor-flow.md) — Vacanti's checklist of behaviours that point to a lack of flow, turned into what each looks like in task text, board state or board history; each sign is a question for the people steering, and one row can only be asked.
- [A Smell Is Not a Finding](reading-history/smell-is-not-a-finding.md) — A sign on a board prompts a check and does not prove a defect; before reporting one as a failure, check whether the project's workflow prevents it, intends it, or limits it to a stage, a kind of task or a property, and say what the sign does not establish.
- [Steps to Predictability](reading-history/steps-to-predictability.md) — Vacanti's four-step summary of the book; set policies on Little's Law's assumptions, collect WIP, Cycle Time and Throughput, visualize them, and act on the analytics.
- [Throughput](reading-history/throughput.md) — Throughput is the count of work items completed per unit of time, in any chosen period; it is not Velocity, which is Story Points per iteration. On a CFD its average over a range is the slope of the bottom line, an exact figure, and each interior line is at once one step's departures and the next step's arrivals, so comparing rates exposes predictability problems and constraints.
- [Triangle on a Scatterplot](reading-history/triangle-on-a-scatterplot.md) — Dots rising in a wedge mean cycle time is growing; it is expected while a process fills from empty, and a defect when it never flattens, from arrivals exceeding departures or from flow debt.
- [Actionable Agile Metrics for Predictability (Vacanti)](reading-history/vacanti-actionable-agile-metrics.md) — Daniel Vacanti's practitioner book arguing that a process becomes predictable by managing flow through Work In Progress, Cycle Time and Throughput rather than by estimating and planning better; it builds from Little's Law through charts, service levels, pull policies and forecasting to one large case, offers no controlled measurement, and its author sells an analytics tool for these metrics.
- [Velocity Masks Unfinished Work](reading-history/velocity-masks-unfinished-work.md) — Points completed can look on plan while features stay unfinished, because velocity counts claimed points and says nothing about how much was started.
- [A Velocity Trend Is Not a Forecast](reading-history/velocity-trend-is-not-a-forecast.md) — Do not project a velocity trend forward; a rise is noted and not planned on, and a decline is a cause to find and remove rather than a rate to plan with.
- [Velocity](reading-history/velocity.md) — The sum of the points of the items completed in an iteration; a rate of completion used both as a retrospective measure and as the forecast for the next iteration, which says nothing about scope change and is not the net progress the source sometimes calls by the same word.
- [Work In Progress](reading-history/work-in-progress.md) — WIP is the count of work items between a process's arrival and departure points; it is counted and not sized, it is not the sum of WIP limits, and it excludes most of the backlog and can be segmented by type.

## Showing Work

- [Bottleneck on the CFD](showing-work/bottleneck-on-the-cfd.md) — A queue band that stays wide on a Cumulative Flow Diagram raises a question about capacity at the next step; per-column Throughput and Cycle Time confirm it, because the chart's shape alone names no bottleneck.
- [Bulging Band on a CFD](showing-work/bulging-band-on-a-cfd.md) — A widening CFD band signals a WIP explosion in that step, whose cause may lie upstream or downstream, and a queue band that bulges or stays thick is the worse case.
- [Burn-Up Chart with Percentile Lines](showing-work/burn-up-with-percentile-lines.md) — A projection chart, which is not a CFD, marked with lines at the release date minus percentile cycle times, so it shows which items still have what chance of making a release.
- [Build a CFD from Entry Dates, Not Counts](showing-work/cfd-built-from-entry-dates.md) — A CFD is derived from the date each item entered each step, not from periodic counts of what sits in each column, because counts subtract when items move back or are removed and lines then fall; counts are safe only if neither ever happens.
- [Cumulative Flow Diagram](showing-work/cumulative-flow-diagram.md) — A chart of cumulative arrivals to and departures from a process over time, with optional bands for the steps between; it carries WIP, approximate average Cycle Time and exact average Throughput at once, but only if it obeys six properties, only about the past, and it cannot show whether what left was any good.
- [Cycle Time Histogram](showing-work/cycle-time-histogram.md) — Bars counting finished items per cycle-time bin; the same data as a scatterplot condensed to show its shape, which in knowledge work is usually a hump on the left and a long right tail, at the cost of all information about when.
- [Cycle Time Scatterplot](showing-work/cycle-time-scatterplot.md) — A chart with one dot per finished item, placed at its finish date and its cycle time; it shows each item's time rather than an average, gives percentiles, the trend across a period and outliers to investigate, and says nothing about work still open.
- [Disappearing Band on a CFD](showing-work/disappearing-band-on-a-cfd.md) — A band that vanishes from a CFD has three candidate causes, a too-coarse reporting interval, a starved step or a skipped step, and they mean different things.
- [Flat Lines on a CFD](showing-work/flat-lines-on-a-cfd.md) — A CFD line that stays horizontal for a long period means zero arrivals or, more often the concern, zero departures, and calls for asking at once why nothing is moving.
- [Gantt Chart at Feature Level](showing-work/gantt-at-feature-level.md) — A Gantt chart is acceptable for showing which features sit in which iteration if it stops at features, runs each bar for the whole iteration, and names no individuals.
- [Iteration Burndown](showing-work/iteration-burndown.md) — A chart of hours remaining by day within an iteration, summed from the board once a day. Cohn finds it useful for iterations of two weeks or longer and unnecessary for one-week ones, where the trend arrives too late.
- [Malformed CFD](showing-work/malformed-cfd.md) — A chart labelled a CFD that breaks its definition, seen as a falling line, a line that falls once later steps are hidden, an outer line that is not arrivals or departures, a graphed backlog whose time the reported Cycle Time leaves out, or a plotted projection; the harm is wrong conclusions about the process and a team that stops trusting the chart.
- [Mismatched Arrivals and Departures](showing-work/mismatched-arrivals-and-departures.md) — When the top CFD line climbs faster than the bottom line, WIP grows, Cycle Time lengthens, and the process is unstable and cannot be predicted.
- [Parking Lot Chart](showing-work/parking-lot-chart.md) — One box per theme in a release, each showing its story count, total estimate and percent complete, so a whole release fits on a page. It shows where progress sits across themes, and not which tasks are done or the trend over time.
- [Points or Time and Count](showing-work/points-or-time-and-count.md) — Which unit a project states progress and forecasts in; Vacanti rejects points and velocity as foreign to customers and silent on what to do, and this wiki resolves it by reader and setup, so outside readers get elapsed time or item count and points may stay inside where the project estimates.
- [Pseudo Control Chart](showing-work/pseudo-control-chart.md) — A cycle time chart with mean and standard-deviation bands labelled UCL and LCL, sold as a Control Chart; it and any percentage printed beside its lines assume normally distributed data that a Histogram of real cycle times does not show, it is pulled by outliers, and it flags items as out of control on that false footing.
- [Reading a Cumulative Flow Diagram](showing-work/reading-a-cfd.md) — A fixed walk over the shapes of a CFD that turns each shape present into a question to check against context, never into a verdict.
- [Reading Flow Balance on a CFD](showing-work/reading-flow-balance-on-a-cfd.md) — A CFD shows arrival and departure rates as slopes, WIP as vertical distance and approximate cycle time as horizontal distance; diverging lines signal imbalance, but a tidy chart proves nothing about health.
- [Release Burndown Bar Chart](showing-work/release-burndown-bar-chart.md) — A burndown drawn as bars whose top tracks completed and re-estimated work, and whose bottom tracks scope added or removed, so the two can be seen apart. More expressive, harder to read, and abandoned at the first argument over which side a change belongs on.
- [Release Burndown Chart](showing-work/release-burndown-chart.md) — A line of work remaining at the start of each iteration that answers how much is left and the net rate and gives a forecast by straight edge; scope growth shows as a rise, it cannot say why progress changed or show risk retired and learning gained, and the forecast assumes nothing changes.
- [S-Curve on a CFD](showing-work/s-curve-on-a-cfd.md) — Between two moments of zero WIP a CFD typically goes flat, steep, flat, and Vacanti argues those flat ends make arrivals and departures hard to match and hurt predictability.
- [Stair Steps on a CFD](showing-work/stair-steps-on-a-cfd.md) — Stair steps on a CFD reveal a batch transfer, regular or not, and the batch is not a defect in itself but a prompt to weigh its effect on predictability.
- [Status Buried in a Long Report](showing-work/status-buried-in-a-long-report.md) — The news that a plan is off track is technically reported but sits where nobody reads it; the sender is responsible for the message being understood, not merely sent.
- [Verifying a Tool's Flow Analytics](showing-work/verifying-tool-flow-analytics.md) — Do not take a tracker's built-in flow charts on trust; derive the numbers from a sample of per-state dates and compare them with what the tool shows.
- [What a CFD Cannot Answer](showing-work/what-a-cfd-cannot-answer.md) — A CFD cannot name a cause or fix, cannot locate a systemic bottleneck, and cannot prove health; a pretty chart can hide a dysfunctional process.
- [Which Chart for Which Plan Question](showing-work/which-chart-for-which-plan-question.md) — Choose the view by the question; iteration burndown for finishing this period, release burndown and velocity for overall progress and forecast, the bar chart for why, a parking lot chart for which themes, a feature Gantt for allocation, and a planned-versus-earned table for what happened.
- [Which View of Cycle Time](showing-work/which-view-of-cycle-time.md) — Choose by the question; a cumulative flow diagram for averages, a scatterplot with percentile lines for how long one item may take and for change over time, a histogram for the shape of the data, and neither for work still open.

## Sizing

- [Buffer Versus Padding](sizing/buffer-versus-padding.md) — Padding is unexplained time hidden inside an estimate, while a buffer is derived margin shown on its own line and added to estimates with local safety removed, and the test is whether the extra can be traced and seen.
- [Choosing How to Estimate Velocity](sizing/choosing-velocity-estimate-approach.md) — Prefer observed iterations, then actuals from a related project by the same team, then a see-what-fits forecast; replace whatever was used with observed values as soon as they exist.
- [Collaborative Task Estimation](sizing/collaborative-task-estimation.md) — Cohn's case that estimates below the story level are also made by more than the presumed doer; the doer is not yet known, others remember past misses, a high number exposes a misunderstanding, and shared estimates are easier to retract.
- [Comparing Estimate to Actual](sizing/comparing-estimate-to-actual.md) — Cohn advises reluctance to compare logged hours against estimates; remaining work is more useful, evaluation pressure can worsen estimates, and variability never goes away. For an agent the pressure and the logging cost fall away, and the variability does not.
- [Completion-Time Distribution](sizing/completion-time-distribution.md) — How long a unit of work takes is a right-skewed range, so a single estimate means nothing until it is known which point on the curve it names; the 50% and 90% points are the two that planning uses.
- [Cone of Uncertainty](sizing/cone-of-uncertainty.md) — Estimates narrow as a project proceeds; Boehm's 0.6x-1.6x at feasibility to +/-15% after requirements, with PMI's asymmetric ranges, all project-level and from sequential or traditional settings. Cohn re-uses the multipliers on velocity, one step per completed iteration from 0.6-1.6 to 0.9-1.1, and admits the mapping has no mathematical basis.
- [Cost per Story Point](sizing/cost-per-story-point.md) — Dividing what a stretch of work cost by the points finished in it turns any estimate into money without logging hours; it is a rough conversion for a keep-or-drop decision, it omits support cost, its labour figures do not transfer to an agent, and costing by points and by whole iterations gives different answers.
- [Dropping Estimates for Flow Forecasts](sizing/dropping-estimates-for-flow-forecasts.md) — Run a flow forecast beside points for a release and test points against Cycle Time on your own history; retire estimates for date forecasting only if the evidence supports it, and keep sizing for cuts.
- [An Estimate Is Not a Promise](sizing/estimate-is-not-a-promise.md) — Nobody is surprised when a game scheduled to end at 4:00 ends at 4:15, yet the same 8% overrun on a twelve-month project is a surprise. A forecast holds up because of the conditions around it, not because it is exact.
- [Estimate Only What May Be Selected](sizing/estimate-only-what-may-be-selected.md) — Every story with a reasonable chance of entering the upcoming release needs an estimate, because estimates are its price; work further out does not need one.
- [Estimate Versus Commitment](sizing/estimate-versus-commitment.md) — An estimate is a probability attached to a date; a commitment is a date chosen after weighing business factors and risks. When the first is taken as the second, the team never gets to make that decision.
- [Estimates as Ranges](sizing/estimates-as-ranges.md) — Early estimates should carry their uncertainty as a range and narrow as uncertainty is removed; a single unqualified date or a precise figure on imprecise work is the sign of ignoring it.
- [Estimating by Horizon](sizing/estimating-by-horizon.md) — Work due in the next few iterations is written small and estimated on the fine scale; more distant or undecided work stays as epics and themes on coarse steps, trading certainty for saved effort, and new work is estimated before the next ordering.
- [Estimating Effort by Purpose](sizing/estimating-effort-by-purpose.md) — How much effort an estimate gets is chosen by the decision it feeds; past a small investment accuracy barely rises, no effort reaches certainty, and a cheap estimate is safe only where delivered results correct it soon.
- [Estimating an Underspecified Item](sizing/estimating-underspecified-work.md) — An item whose details are missing still gets a size; state assumptions, guess from the plausible range, and move on, without treating the estimate as evidence that the item is ready.
- [Estimation Baseline](sizing/estimation-baseline.md) — A set of reference stories, agreed in one unit, that gives estimates the same meaning whoever makes them; built from finished work or from a mix of new stories, and then used by analogy.
- [Estimation Scale](sizing/estimation-scale.md) — Estimates sit on a small predefined non-linear scale, kept for near-term work within about one order of magnitude, because gaps must grow with uncertainty; a step is a bucket, an estimate moves only by a step, and a value between steps, or a split reconciled to its original by arithmetic, is false precision.
- [Estimation Techniques](sizing/estimation-techniques.md) — The three ways of deriving an estimate, expert opinion, analogy and disaggregation, what each is good and bad at, and why Cohn combines them; which applies depends on whether comparable estimated work exists.
- [Executor-Bound Estimates](sizing/executor-bound-estimates.md) — A duration estimate is true only for the person who gave it, so two people can both be right, have no way to settle on one number, and the estimate fails when the work changes hands.
- [Forecast Velocity by Seeing What Fits](sizing/forecast-velocity-by-what-fits.md) — When no history exists and no iteration can run, expand a representative sample of stories into estimated tasks until available capacity fills, then range the resulting points; the hours arithmetic is human and does not transfer to an agent.
- [Hidden WIP in Large Items](sizing/hidden-wip-in-large-items.md) — WIP counts items and not work, so one large task can hold several tasks' worth of work under a count of one; the sign is a cycle time outlier or a task whose text lists separable results.
- [Hindsight Re-Estimation](sizing/hindsight-re-estimation.md) — Raising the estimates of finished tasks after they ran long, while open tasks stay on the old scale, inflates velocity and mixes two scales, so the forecast pulls in without any more work done.
- [When Historical Velocity Can Be Reused](sizing/historical-velocity-comparability.md) — Past velocity carries over only when little has changed; seven questions test it, and any no means either setting the history aside or widening its range to 60-160%.
- [Ideal-Day Estimate Decay](sizing/ideal-day-estimate-decay.md) — Estimates in ideal days fall as the executor gets better, so equal work carries different numbers and velocity stays flat while output grows, which hides the improvement.
- [Ideal Days Compared to Actual Days](sizing/ideal-days-compared-to-actual-days.md) — Because an ideal day looks like a day, it gets compared with real days; teams end up justifying the gap, and under pressure the unit is quietly redefined into elapsed time.
- [Ideal Days as a Measure of Size](sizing/ideal-days.md) — An ideal day estimates a task's size while ignoring the environment's overhead, so it converts to duration through velocity just as story points do. Its weakness is that the unit reads like a calendar day.
- [Ideal Estimate Read as a Deadline](sizing/ideal-estimate-read-as-deadline.md) — A number meant as uninterrupted work gets counted off on a calendar, so the date is wrong from the moment it is written. The sign is a date derived from an estimate with no conversion through velocity.
- [Ideal Time Versus Elapsed Time](sizing/ideal-time-vs-elapsed-time.md) — Ideal time is how long work takes stripped of everything around it; elapsed time is what passes on the calendar. Ideal time is much easier to predict, and the gap between them is overhead, not work.
- [Independent Estimates](sizing/independent-estimates.md) — Estimators commit before seeing each other's numbers, and a spread is treated as evidence that they read different work into the text, not as noise to average; what remains of planning poker once its meeting script is removed.
- [Do My Work Items All Need to Be the Same Size?
