(Kanban Playbook)](sizing/kanban-playbook-right-sizing.md) — An unsigned ProKanban playbook page replacing estimation with one question, will this item likely finish within the SLE, and offering four ways to split; its mechanisms are kept, while its figures are illustrations and its central claim needs correcting.
- [Local Safety](sizing/local-safety.md) — The extra time between a task's 50% and 90% estimates; summed across tasks it produces a plan far longer than needed, because all tasks do not go wrong on the same run, and it protects tasks rather than the deadline that matters.
- [One Estimate per Task, Not One per Role](sizing/one-estimate-per-task.md) — Give each task a single aggregate estimate. Per-role estimates force velocity and remaining work to be tracked per role, which is rarely worth it unless roles truly cannot substitute for one another.
- [Over-Disaggregation](sizing/over-disaggregation.md) — Splitting an item in order to estimate it helps until it can be compared, but past that point pieces go missing with no check that would show it and summed ranges grow too wide to use.
- [Overrun Triggers a Recut](sizing/overrun-triggers-a-recut.md) — A task running past the expectation set for its size is a signal to act on the task itself, not to wait longer.
- [Parkinson's Law](sizing/parkinsons-law.md) — Work expands to fill the time allowed, so a stated duration acts as permission and early finishes rarely appear; the mechanism is human, and only its visible form, additions nobody asked for, may survive an agent, for a different reason.
- [Re-estimate Remaining Work](sizing/re-estimate-remaining-work.md) — An estimate of what is left on an open item is changed the moment someone learns it is wrong, and one far off is replaced by two or three items; the trigger is discovery, earlier than an overrun, and a whole task's size step follows a stricter rule.
- [Re-Estimate Only When Relative Size Changes](sizing/re-estimate-when-relative-size-changes.md) — An estimate is changed when a task's size relative to other tasks has changed, not because the task took longer than expected; slow progress is absorbed by velocity, and a lesson about a class of work is applied to the whole class.
- [Right-Sizing](sizing/right-sizing.md) — Before pulling an item, ask one yes/no question; can it finish within the SLE? Yes means pull it; no means split it, reduce its fidelity, or spike it. This replaces item-level points on a project that has an SLE.
- [Run Iterations to Observe Velocity](sizing/run-iterations-to-observe-velocity.md) — The default way to estimate velocity is to hold the number back for one to three iterations and measure; this buys a founded estimate at the cost of giving no figure at the start.
- [Similar Tasks Overrun Together](sizing/similar-tasks-overrun-together.md) — Durations of similar tasks are correlated, so when the first overruns the rest are likely to, and errors do not cancel; revise the siblings' estimates instead of expecting to make up the time.
- [Single-Date Plan](sizing/single-date-plan.md) — A plan reduced to one date loses the assumptions behind it and cannot be judged; a usable forecast gives a range, the near-term work, its assumptions and how progress will be measured.
- [Size Ceiling](sizing/size-ceiling.md) — The size above which a task is cut, chosen by whether its scope can still be stated, with the sources' figures kept alongside the setting that produced them; a ratio of the period under iterations, the likelihood of finishing inside the SLE under a flow setup, and a floor as well as a ceiling. A large item is read as a placeholder to be replaced once understood.
- [Size Spread](sizing/size-spread.md) — Tasks near the top of the order are kept small and within about one order of magnitude of each other, because similar sizes reduce variability in cycle time and estimate better; work further out stays large until it nears the top.
- [Separate Size from Duration](sizing/size-versus-duration.md) — Estimate how big the work is first, in a unit that cannot be read as time, and obtain how long it takes from a measured rate, so that a wrong rate does not invalidate the size estimates; a size given in hours, or a date with no size and rate behind it, shows the two have been confused.
- [Story Points Do Not Convert to Hours](sizing/story-points-do-not-convert-to-hours.md) — A points-to-hours factor holds only as an average over many items; per item the hours form a distribution, so some one-point stories take longer than some two-point stories. A fixed conversion is the defect.
- [Story Points or Ideal Days](sizing/story-points-or-ideal-days.md) — Which unit to estimate in; Cohn prefers story points because they are a pure measure of size, and allows ideal days as a starting point or where an early velocity forecast is needed.
- [Story Points](sizing/story-points.md) — A unitless, relative measure of the overall size of a piece of work; only the ratios between items carry meaning, and the unit gains a time meaning only through velocity. Because it describes only how much there is to do, it is estimated by analogy, needs comparators, covers the whole task and not the estimator's part, does not change as the executor improves, and cannot be held against the calendar.
- [Summed Role Estimates](sizing/summed-role-estimates.md) — An estimate built by adding what each specialty thinks its part takes treats a task as separate pieces, where a single whole-task number forces discussion of everything involved.
- [Triangulation](sizing/triangulation.md) — Estimate a task by comparing it with several already-estimated tasks, one a step smaller and one a step larger, not with a single baseline; the comparison set is what keeps a scale step meaning one thing.
- [Unknowns Surfaced by Estimating](sizing/unknowns-surfaced-by-estimating.md) — Estimating exposes what nobody knows; the unknown is then either resolved by learning now, or noted and reflected in a larger estimate or a range.
- [A Velocity Estimate Is a Range](sizing/velocity-estimate-range.md) — State estimated velocity as a range sized to the evidence behind it, never as one number; a date computed from a single velocity figure inherits a precision nobody has.
- [Velocity Self-Correction](sizing/velocity-self-correction.md) — Because points are relative, a shared misjudgement of size or rate shows up as a different observed velocity and corrects the forecast without re-estimating, so consistency matters more than correctness; it covers shared error, not error in the ratios, and only while estimates stay untouched and the rate stays stable.
- [Who Estimates](sizing/who-estimates.md) — Estimates come from the group that may do the work and not from a single expert, because the executor is not known in advance and others catch what the expert forgets; with an agent executor the first reason goes and the second is what survives.

## Task Content

- [Agent Silence Is Not Completeness](task-content/agent-silence-is-not-completeness.md) — An agent not asking a question does not show the task was complete; readiness is judged from the task and the repository, and telling the agent to ask is not a substitute.
- [All Work to Finished Is in the Plan](task-content/all-work-to-finished-is-in-the-plan.md) — A plan names everything between a story and a working, tested, documented result, and nothing that does not add value to this project; work kept off the plan by habit stays there only if the executor really has the habit.
- [Ambig-SWE (Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity)](task-content/ambig-swe.md) — A benchmark study of six LLM models given deliberately stripped software issues; it measures how well agents detect missing information, ask for it, and use the answers, on synthetic underspecification against a simulated user.
- [Conditions of Satisfaction](task-content/conditions-of-satisfaction.md) — The criteria by which the product owner will judge a release or a feature; they carry schedule, scope and resources at release level, with one factor usually preeminent, and high-level tests at iteration level, where a story is finished when shown to meet all of them and they are written ahead only for stories likely to be taken next; a graded word in a title is pinned by a condition on the task and not by another task, and planning repeats on a lessened set when they cannot all be met.
- [The Conversation Moves Into the Task](task-content/conversation-moves-into-the-task.md) — What a human team settles by talking during development has to be settled before an agent starts and written into the task; a text that points at a conversation or at memory is the sign it was not.
- [Empty Fields](task-content/empty-fields.md) — An empty field is a failure only at the stage where the workflow reads it, and only for fields something depends on; practitioners split on missing properties for exactly these reasons, and a filled field does not prove a real value.
- [Fact Stranded Outside the Task](task-content/fact-stranded-outside-the-task.md) — A decision or value that is known and recorded somewhere other than the task, such as a comment or a chat; practitioners called it problematic with no one disagreeing, and the sign is a field or text contradicted by what was said elsewhere.
- [Recoverable Versus Task-Only Facts](task-content/recoverable-versus-task-only-facts.md) — A fact the executor cannot recover from the repository must be in the task; a fact it can recover is welcome but does not hold a task back from being ready.
- [A Task Must Justify Itself](task-content/task-must-justify-itself.md) — A task states why it exists and how it contributes to the larger result; a reason that only restates the action, or pieces that do not add up, is the sign it does not.
- [Testable Acceptance](task-content/testable-acceptance.md) — A task states what would show it done in a form that can be checked; a requester who cannot say how to test it is a sign with three possible diagnoses.
- [Underspecified Task](task-content/underspecified-task.md) — A task missing information an expert would need to succeed; distinct from an ambiguous one, and more dangerous with an agent because the agent tends to proceed instead of asking.
- [User Story](task-content/user-story.md) — A brief description of functionality as a user sees it, kept lightweight by deferring detail to conversation; that deferral is what does not carry over to an agent executor.
- [INVEST in Good Stories, and SMART Tasks (Wake)](task-content/wake-invest.md) — Bill Wake's 2003 article naming six characteristics of a good story and five of a good task; the origin of INVEST, with no measurement behind it.
- [Whoever Writes the Plan Controls It](task-content/whoever-writes-the-plan-controls-it.md) — The hand that records a plan can change it; Cohn saw an agreed 12-hour estimate entered as 8, and an agreed decision typed as a vague task so that it stayed open. The record then differs from what was decided.

## Work States

- [Active Versus Queued](work-states/active-versus-queued.md) — A board has to show whether a task is being worked on or is ready and waiting for attention, because an active column that hides queued work makes bottlenecks unreadable; this kind of waiting is inside the project and is not the outside wait of the parking lot.
- [Arrival Point](work-states/arrival-point.md) — A process needs one explicit point at which work counts as WIP; on most boards it is a WIP-limited first column that signals commitment and is not a backlog.
- [Backlog Versus Commitment](work-states/backlog-versus-commitment.md) — A backlog is a container of candidates, not committed or prioritized work; commitment happens when capacity exists, so a backlog belongs inside a process's boundaries, and on its CFD, only if it really has been committed, a choice that moves the start of Cycle Time.
- [Column Doneness Criteria](work-states/column-doneness-criteria.md) — Each column states what must be true before a story leaves it, so quality steps are enforced at the move and not remembered; the last column's Done also fixes what the metrics cover.
- [Column Versus Attribute](work-states/column-versus-attribute.md) — A column is for a stage that happens in a predictable place, after which work goes forward; anything fleeting that can land anywhere is an attribute marked on the task where it stands. A handoff passes the test and a block does not.
- [Departure Point](work-states/departure-point.md) — A process needs one exact point past which work no longer counts as WIP; it must be counted even if it is not visualized.
- [Distinguishable Work States](work-states/distinguishable-work-states.md) — The sources give criteria and no canonical column set, and they treat a fixed list as the failure case; what they do support is a small set of distinctions any board must let a reader make, drawn partly as columns and partly as markers.
- [Iteration Task Board](work-states/iteration-task-board.md) — Cohn's board for one iteration, with a row per story and columns To Do, Tests Ready, In Process, To Verify and Hours; only To Do and In Process are required states, and the rest are a marker, an optional handoff and a computed total.
- [Judging a Board's Columns](work-states/judging-board-columns.md) — The criteria for auditing a board's columns, each with the sign of failing it; six are judged per column and four across the board, and they apply to any setup with states.
- [Where Do We Start When Choosing Workflow States? (Kanban Playbook)](work-states/kanban-playbook-workflow-states.md) — An unsigned ProKanban playbook page saying states should be derived from how work actually moved, not from a familiar column list; it separates states from activities and treats a five-column default as the failure case. It reports no measurement.
- [Mapping Workflow States](work-states/mapping-workflow-states.md) — Derive a board's states by tracing recent tasks of different kinds, listing what actually happened to them, noting what was skipped and where they waited, and grouping similar activities; the states are containers and the activities are what happen inside them.
- [Process Boundaries](work-states/process-boundaries.md) — Naming where work arrives and departs is the first act of adopting flow metrics, and crossings are counted on the date they happen, whatever an iteration is doing; where each point belongs is settled on started-and-finished-points.
- [Should We Include Waiting or Blocked Items in WIP Limits?](work-states/radzikowska-waiting-blocked.md) — A Kanban Maturity Model answer to whether stopped work counts toward WIP limits; blocked items stay and count, items waiting on outsiders may be parked, and a parked item past its time becomes blocked.
- [Started and Finished Points](work-states/started-and-finished-points.md) — The two defined moments between which a task counts as work in progress, which Vacanti calls a process's arrival and departure points; every flow metric hangs from them, so each has to be an event the board can show and not a claim by the executor. The Kanban Guide lets each workflow define them, the Scrum Guide fixes only finished, as one Definition of Done, and arrival is the first pull in a pull system and a stakeholder's expectation in a push system.
- [Waiting Versus Blocked](work-states/waiting-versus-blocked.md) — Stopped work is waiting if an outside party holds it, an expected end is known and nothing can shorten it; otherwise, or once that end has passed, it is blocked.
- [Designing Your Board to Focus on Flow (Wester)](work-states/wester-board-design.md) — Julia Wester's practice post on board design, from a metrics vendor's blog; five tips with no measurement, of which the mechanisms are kept and any implied size of effect is not. It supplies the test separating a column from an attribute.
- [When an Arrivals Column Is Needed](work-states/when-an-arrivals-column-is-needed.md) — An explicit arrivals column is optional when work can be pulled ad hoc without outside coordination; balance then comes from constant WIP alone.
